newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Renault faces crunch union vote.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Renault faces crunch union vote.

text.p: Workers at the doomed Belgian plant of French car maker Renault SA decide on Thursday morning whether to continue their strike against the plant's impending closure or return to work.

The 3,100 employees of the Renault Industrie Belgique assembly plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels will vote in a ballot 0400 GMT and 0900 GMT to either resume work or to continue their five-week stoppage.
The result is due after 1000 GMT.
"It will be a close thing," Vilvoorde CMB metal workers union leader Karel Gacoms told Reuters.

"For the workers it will be a tough decision: continue a known union strategy and strike until the bitter end or go back to work, occupy part of the plant and stage occassional protests," he said in a telephone interview.

Since group headquarters announced the decision in late February to close the plant by July, workers have held billions of francs worth of finished cars hostage, hoping to use them as bargaining chips in any negotiations with management.
Loss-making Renault is closing the plant to tackle overcapacity and rising costs.

Vilvoorde unions recommend a resumption of work at the profitable and efficient plant -- a move analysts see as part of a strategy to begin lengthy negotiations with management on the terms and conditions of the mass dismissal of the workers.
Unions have condemned Renault's decision, which they say broke Belgian, French and European Union labour laws since the company failed to inform and consult workers adequately.
Belgian and French courts have ruled the closure procedure followed by Renault illegal and ordered the company to play it by the book, handing the unions a moral victory.

In answer to the rulings, the unions have called a referendum, working on the assumption that since the courts have re-set the clocks to February 26 -- the day before the Renault decision -- workers should do the same and return to work.

Analysts say that Renault chief executive officer Louis Schweitzer would use a continued strike to his advantage, claiming that the workers did not want to play by the rules or even that their unwillingness to work only underlined the need for the plant to be shut down.
After the ballot on Thursday Renault workers will travel to the car assembly plants of Ford, Volkswagen, Volvo and Opel in Belgium to call for support and hand out pamphlets.

Gacoms said that after the court rulings, which Renault has said it is appealing, unions had decided to take legal action to force the company to pay out wages to the workers for the duration of the strike since formally they had remained on the Renault payroll.
Workers would re-pay the unions any strike money received.
A conservative estimate put the sum involved for Renault at some 65 million Belgian francs.

Gacoms said it was unclear how long any negotiations on the terms and conditions of the closure would take. "The court appeals could take until the end of April, only then the procedure would start." The actual closure of Vilvoorde would likely be later than July.
